source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Defines epistemic action: a physical action that makes mental computation easier, faster or more reliable. Tetris players rotate falling pieces more than needed to place them.
numbers: Physical rotation of a zoid takes as few as 100 ms; mental rotation of 90 degrees is estimated at 800-1200 ms (pilot Shepard-Metzler-style task, three Tetris players). Early rotation shows the hidden part of a zoid 150-300 ms sooner; a zoid falls one square per 150 ms at medium speed. Rotations exceed the count needed for pure placement in every zoid type (their Fig 6).
quote: physical actions that make mental computation easier, faster, or more reliable
limits: Small sample, a game task, pilot data for the mental rotation timing. Epistemic purpose is inferred, not measured directly.
agent_relevance: An external step the code runs (render, test, reformat) can replace a costly internal step in the model. Give the model cheap actions that reveal state before it commits.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action (interleaving argument)
finding: Argues players interleave action and thought instead of planning fully then acting; false starts are cheap. Classical plan-then-act planners cannot explain the epistemic moves.
numbers: Keystroke gap at least 75 ms, average about 250 ms; a false start costs 75-750 ms, so acting early is cheap.
limits: Argument from timing, not a fitted model.
agent_relevance: Supports cheap probing steps (run, look, adjust) over long one-shot planning, as long as each probe is cheap and reversible (fits G3).

source: Kirsh (1995) The intelligent use of space
finding: Classifies how people arrange the workplace to cut thinking: simplify choice, simplify perception, save internal computation. Data come from videos of cooking, assembly and packing, supermarket observation and Tetris studies.
numbers: No effect sizes in the opened text; classification from observation.
limits: Qualitative. The author notes psychologists rarely let subjects manipulate the stimulus.
agent_relevance: Three jobs for the code layer: shrink the choice set, make the key feature visible, store intermediate results outside the model.

source: Clark & Chalmers (1998) The extended mind
finding: Parity principle: if an external process works like an internal one, it is part of the cognitive process. Otto (Alzheimer's, notebook) is the test case.
numbers: No empirical numbers; philosophical argument.
quote: For Otto, his notebook plays the role usually played by a biological memory.
limits: Philosophy, not data. Critics dispute that a notebook is cognition (not in the opened text).
agent_relevance: If the code store is always available, trusted and read automatically, design it as part of the agent's memory. If not, treat it as a tool.

source: Norman (1991) Cognitive artifacts (chapter in Carroll, Designing Interaction)
finding: NOT OPENED (PDF not reachable). Remembered claim, unverified: artifacts change the task the person faces rather than amplify the person; system view and personal view differ.
numbers: not verified
limits: Do not cite details from this line until the chapter is read.
agent_relevance: Check whether the code-plus-model system faces a different task than the model alone.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: NOT OPENED (HTTP 403). Remembered claim, unverified: the cockpit system (pilots, speed card booklet, airspeed indicator bugs) remembers and computes the speeds.
numbers: not verified
limits: Field case study, no quantitative test.
agent_relevance: Design code and model as one memory system, with stored cards doing the remembering.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: NOT OPENED (PDF not reachable). Remembered design, unverified: Tower of Hanoi isomorphs with rules held in the display versus in the head.
numbers: not verified
limits: Exact times, errors and N must be checked in the paper.
agent_relevance: Rules shown in the interface instead of held in prompt memory may lower error. Test directly.

source: Larkin & Simon (1987) Why a diagram is (sometimes) worth ten thousand words
finding: NOT OPENED. Remembered claim, unverified: diagram and sentence can hold the same facts but differ in search and recognition cost.
numbers: not verified
limits: Computational models, not human experiments with numbers.
agent_relevance: Format of context changes search cost for the model too; see the format lines below.

source: Hesselmann (2020) No conclusive evidence for a Google Stroop effect (PeerJ replication of Sparrow et al. 2011)
finding: Replicated Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Exp 1 with a design close to the original. No evidence that hard trivia questions prime internet words.
numbers: N=89 analysed (117 tested); Bayes factor 5.07 for the null; BF 16.43 for the null against the original's specific pattern; t(88) = -1.04, p = .301; all 117 participants: BF01 = 9.31. Original reported F(1,66) = 5.02, p < .03.
limits: Original authors gave no materials to the earlier replication; Sparrow (2018) objected to its design. Hesselmann changed the design in response and still found no effect.
agent_relevance: Weak support for the claim that access to a store changes how people think. Do not build on the Google effect.

source: Camerer et al. (2018), as described in Hesselmann (2020): replication of Sparrow et al. 2011 Exp 1
finding: Failed replication of the Google Stroop effect in the Nature/Science replicability project, with adequate power.
numbers: Per Hesselmann: no significant effect despite adequate statistical power; two replication attempts failed.
limits: Seen only through a secondary paper, not the replication report itself.
agent_relevance: Same as above.

source: Direct replication of Ward et al. (2017) Exp 2, Reexamining the Brain Drain effect (2021)
finding: Pre-registered replication with six conditions (phone on desk, in bag, outside room; power on or off). The brain drain effect did not replicate.
numbers: No difference between phone-location conditions on operation span or go/no-go. Sample size not in the opened abstract.
limits: Only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Mere presence of an unused external device does not drain thought. Costs appear when the store is used or its trust changes.

source: Ngai & Gilbert (2026) Metacognitive training facilitates optimal cognitive offloading
finding: People over-use external reminders even when memory would earn more. Low confidence in memory drives it. Predictions plus feedback in 5 trials improved calibration and reminder choice; predictions alone did not.
numbers: Exp 1 N=164, Exp 2 N=416 (replicated). Underconfidence fell from M=-14.5 (SD 23.3) to M=-6.3 (SD 16.3), F(1,162)=28.5, partial eta2=.15. Group x Time F(1,162)=4.3, p=.039, eta2=.026. Exp 2 group effect F(3,412)=8.98, p<.001, eta2=.06.
limits: Online points task; everyday effect untested. Earlier metacognitive interventions gave mixed results.
agent_relevance: The agent should choose when to use a tool by calibrated confidence, not habit. Feed back tool-versus-no-tool outcomes (G3, G7).

source: Ngai & Gilbert (2026), background review of intention offloading
finding: Reminders are highly effective: in lab tasks they cut memory errors by an order of magnitude or more (Gilbert et al. 2020). Over-use of reminders is common and stable within a person over time.
numbers: Cited studies: Gilbert 2020; Ball 2022; Froscher 2022; Kirk 2021; Sachdeva & Gilbert 2020, 2024. Exact figures not in the opened text.
limits: Secondary citation; underlying papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Offloading helps most. The risk is the wrong choice of when to offload.

source: Dupre & Ball (2026) Let it go: how trusted reminders alter intention maintenance
finding: After experiencing 100% reliable reminders, people think less about the intention while waiting, shift attention to the ongoing task, and retrieve less when the reminder is withdrawn. Reminders were duplicative at first, then substitutive.
numbers: N=320; reliability crossed 0/50/100% with reminder present or absent. Session 1: reminders raised performance without cutting prospective-memory thoughts. Session 2: the 100% group reduced PM thoughts and retrieved less when reminders were unexpectedly removed.
limits: Student sample, lab task; effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: If the agent trusts a store it stops maintaining the item itself. If the code layer can fail, say so in the prompt or add a fallback.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your brain on ChatGPT
finding: Essay writing with an LLM, a search engine or no tool over 3 sessions, then a fourth with groups swapped. LLM users showed the weakest EEG connectivity, lowest ownership, and could not quote their own essays.
numbers: 54 participants (18 per group) in sessions 1-3; 18 in session 4. 83.3% (15/18) of LLM users failed to quote correctly vs 11.1% (2/18) in each of the search and brain-only groups. LLM-to-Brain: weaker connectivity; Brain-to-LLM: higher recall and wider reactivation.
quote: The LLM group also fell behind in their ability to quote from the essays they wrote just minutes prior.
limits: Preprint, small N, EEG inference, essay task.
agent_relevance: A tool that writes the answer leaves no trace of the work in the user. For the agent: keep the model's own step in the loop (G1, G2).

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: agent-computer interfaces enable automated software engineering
finding: Defines the agent-computer interface (ACI) as the layer between a fixed model and the computer. Interface design alone changes success.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo: SWE-agent 12.47% (286/2,294) full SWE-bench; 18.00% (54/300) Lite. RAG 1.31% full, 2.67% Lite. Shell-only 11.00% Lite, so the ACI gives a 64% relative gain. HumanEvalFix pass@1 87.7% Python vs GPT-4 47.0%.
limits: One model family, SWE-bench; ACI tuned by hand on a dev split. Cost 8-13x RAG.
agent_relevance: The direct match for our code-model interface: fixed model, better interface, large gain.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent ablations (Table 3, SWE-bench Lite, GPT-4 Turbo)
finding: Each interface part matters. Edit with linting beats edit without; summarised search beats none; a 100-line viewer beats 30 lines and the full file.
numbers: Editor: no edit 10.3%, edit 15.0%, edit with linting 18.0%. Search: iterative 12.0%, none 15.7%, summarised 18.0%. Viewer: 30 lines 14.3%, 100 lines 18.0%, full file 12.7%. Context: last 5 observations 18.0%, full history 15.0%. No demo 16.3%.
limits: Single run on 300 tasks; 1-3 point gaps are near noise.
agent_relevance: Guardrail feedback at the point of error, concise output and trimmed history raised success. Matches G2.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: human UIs make poor ACIs
finding: Iterative search copied from IDE interfaces made the agent step through every hit and did worse than no search tool.
numbers: Iterative search 12.0% vs no search 15.7% (Lite). Shell chains of cd, ls, cat described as very inefficient.
limits: Observation on one model.
agent_relevance: Do not hand the model human interfaces. Design against model weaknesses such as exhaustive stepping.

source: Yao et al. (2022) ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models
finding: Interleaving thought and tool action beats acting without thought. Without thoughts, Act fails to break goals into subgoals and loses track of state.
numbers: ALFWorld: best ReAct 71% vs best Act 45% and BUTLER 37%; worst ReAct trial 48% beats the best of both; relative gain over Act 33% to 90%, average 62% over six trials. Absolute gains over IL/RL: +34% ALFWorld, +10% WebShop.
limits: Few-shot prompts; PaLM-540B; synthetic and web-shop settings.
agent_relevance: Fits Kirsh and Maglio: acts interleaved with thought. Supports the attempt, check, revise loop.

source: Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer
finding: A 6.7B model (GPT-J) trained to call tools beats baselines and some much larger models on factual lookup; it picks the QA tool in 98.1% of LAMA cases.
numbers: LAMA: best GPT-J baseline improved by 11.7, 5.2 and 18.6 points (SQuAD, Google-RE, T-REx). Tool choice: 98.1% QA tool, 0.7% other, 1.2% none. GPT-J SQuAD/Google-RE/T-REx without tools: 17.8 / 4.9 / 31.9. Math table was garbled in extraction and is not recorded.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, outside our no-training constraint. Wikipedia search withheld on LAMA.
agent_relevance: A model can learn when to ask for help. With prompting only, the code must decide when.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Executable code actions elicit better LLM agents (CodeAct)
finding: Acting by writing code, rather than JSON or text tool calls, raises success and cuts steps, because code has control flow and data flow.
numbers: Up to 20% higher success and up to 30% fewer actions on M3ToolEval (17 LLMs tested on API-Bank and their own benchmark); gains widen with model capability.
limits: Per-model numbers not read.
agent_relevance: The action format is part of the interface. A code action space lets one step do the work of several.

source: Tam et al. (2024) Let me speak freely? Format restrictions and LLM reasoning
finding: Forcing structured output (JSON, XML, YAML) hurts reasoning, more so as constraints tighten. Parsing errors do not explain it.
numbers: LLaMA-3-8B Last Letter: 0.148% parsing error in JSON but a 38.15% performance gap across formats. Gemini 1.5 Flash and GPT-3.5 Turbo had near-zero parse failures. Classification tasks can gain from format restriction.
limits: Tasks include GSM8K and Last Letter; effect depends on model and task.
agent_relevance: Interface format taxes the model. Let it reason in free text and have code extract the answer.

source: He et al. (2024) Does prompt formatting have any impact on LLM performance?
finding: The same content in plain text, Markdown, JSON or YAML changes accuracy sharply; the best format differs by model and task.
numbers: Up to 40% change on a code translation task; one GPT-3.5 benchmark changed by over 200%; a 42% rise for JSON over Markdown in the paper's MMLU international-law example. GPT-4 was more consistent.
limits: Figures read from abstract and early text, not mapped to tables.
agent_relevance: Layout is a model-specific interface choice and must be tested, not assumed (G7).

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the middle
finding: Accuracy depends on where the relevant fact sits in the context: best at start or end, worst in the middle.
numbers: Multi-document QA: GPT-3.5-Turbo falls by more than 20% when the answer is in the middle; with 20 or 30 documents it drops below its closed-book 56.1%. Oracle: 88.3% GPT-3.5-Turbo, 76.1% Claude-1.3.
limits: 2023-era models; later long-context models may differ.
agent_relevance: Where the code places each fact in the prompt is artifact design. Put key facts and checks at the ends.

source: Hsieh et al. (2023) Tool documentation enables zero-shot tool usage
finding: Short tool documentation is enough to teach tool use and beats demonstrations across hundreds of tools.
numbers: 6 tasks, vision and text. Zero-shot with docs matches few-shot demos on existing benchmarks; on a new dataset with hundreds of APIs, docs without demos beat demos without docs.
limits: Exact table numbers not read; document length matters (their Fig 7).
agent_relevance: Write a short, precise manual for every code tool the model can call.

source: Synthesis across lines in this file (author inference, not a source)
finding: The interface shapes the work as much as the model. Supported levers: cheap probes, concise point-of-error feedback, calibrated offloading, stable format and position. Documented human risk: trust in a store reduces self-maintenance. Famous Google and phone effects did not replicate.
numbers: none
limits: Human offloading studies are lab tasks; LLM studies are mostly single-benchmark.
agent_relevance: Treat as hypotheses; each element must win at equal tokens (G7).
